{"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18449v1.pdf", "scope": "bounded PDF text extraction from up to 24 pages; figures, tables, equations, layout, and scanned-image text may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents
for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
Yibo Wen1,Han Liu 1
on behalf of the Autonomous Science Bench Team
1Northwestern University
Abstract.AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a
limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active
experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduceAutonomous Science Bench, an initial release
comprising six budgeted design–build–test–learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology,
chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service,
and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires
passing two calibrated gates: adiscoverygate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and alearning
gate, which evaluates its model’s ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent–model
configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is
solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate
rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen
designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1
of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard athttps://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.
Correspondence:hanliu@northwestern.edu
